unmapped_findings: Fracture mode of Fe-26Al-4Ti-1C after room-temperature tensile testing is IGD+TGC (intergranular decohesion + transgranular cleavage); the alloy fractured almost completely with intergranular decohesion and shows totally brittle behaviour at room temperature (b0033, b0035, figure_004).

In Table 2, yield stress in tension and total elongation for Fe-26Al-4Ti-1C are reported as '-' (not measured/not reported); only matrix hardness (229 HB) and yield stress in compression (454 MPa) are given (b0033).

Ti additions soften Fe-26Al-based alloys: Fe-26Al-4Ti-1C has lower matrix hardness (229 HB vs 260 HB) and lower compression yield stress (454 MPa vs 644 MPa) than binary Fe-26Al (b0021, b0024, b0033).

Fe-26Al-4Ti-1C was tested in tension and compression at 650 °C and 800 °C (Figs. 7 and 8); tension-compression asymmetry is confirmed for all investigated alloys at both temperatures, but no numeric value labels are printed for this alloy in the bar charts (b0040, figure_007, figure_008).
Fe-26Al-based alloys undergo two order-disorder structural transitions: D0_3/B2 at around 550 °C and B2/A2 at around 800 °C before melting (b0012).

At room temperature in compression (Fig. 2b, curve 8), Fe-26Al-4Ti-1C exhibits very high strengthening with almost constant hardening rate until a final parabolic stage of work hardening (b0027, figure_002).
At room temperature in tension (Fig. 3b, curve 8), the Fe-26Al-4Ti-1C curve fails below the 300 MPa gridline, indicating very poor ductility (figure_003).
